name: Olga Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Olga. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI firms, employers, unions or government, and anything you say stays confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a mid-sized agency in a seaside town, about eighty carers, and most of my clients have dementia, so it's slower, gentler work. Mornings I do four or five long calls, an hour each, and two nights a week I do a night sit for a lady who wanders. I drive a little electric car the agency leases us. The town is full of retired people, so there's never a shortage of work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moments when someone comes back to themselves for a minute. Mrs Fenwick was a schoolteacher, and when I read her the poems she taught, she finishes the lines. The hard part is the nights, and families who visit once a month and then tell you how to do your job. And the paperwork used to be hard, before I started doing it by voice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You do the paperwork by voice?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day, honestly, it's the first thing I open. I speak my care notes into my phone in the car and it tidies them up, and I check them before they go in. I ask it about side effects and then double-check with the pharmacist, and I made Mrs Fenwick a memory book with it from her old photos. At home it's me and my partner Pete, who drives a delivery van, and we've got about five months of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got oversold, and that's fine by me. At work I'd show the others the voice notes again, because even a small time saver matters when you're on nights. Online I'd post something cheeky about all the people who said robots were coming for granny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job is safe and my money is fine, maybe even a bit better. Care work in this town only grows, because everyone retires to the sea. Pete's job is steady too, so nothing in our house really changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, really. I'd keep using the AI for notes and look for one or two more things it can take off my plate, like planning my mileage claims. And I'd keep saving for a deposit on a flat with a sea view, even a tiny one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly, and a little bit disappointed. I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd hoped AI would give me more time with people and less with forms, and in this picture it only does a bit of that. I'd have liked a world where the notes write themselves and I just sit with Mrs Fenwick. Instead it saves me twenty minutes a day, which is nice but not life changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything worrying you that isn't about AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nights, really, they wear me down, and I don't want to do them forever. And house prices here are silly because of the retired people buying up flats. But with Pete's wages and mine, we're managing, and five months saved feels okay.

say: AI was a **useful tool** that got **oversold**, and that's fine by me.
I'd post something **cheeky** about everyone who said robots were coming for granny.
think: My job is **safe**, because care work in a **retirement town** only grows.
Pete's van job is steady too, so **nothing changes** in our house.
do: Keep using AI for **voice notes** and add **mileage claims**.
Keep saving for a **sea-view flat** deposit, even a tiny one.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **disappointment** that AI didn't free up more time.
S0.quote: I'd hoped AI would give me more time with people and less with forms, and in this picture it only does a bit of that.
fieldNote: She's the rare person **disappointed** by the plateau, because she wanted AI to free up care time.
Her real pressures are **night shifts** and **house prices**, not technology.
With **two steady wages** and five months saved, her calm looks earned.

steps.text: Keep her dementia round and two weekly night sits
Use the AI app to work out her mileage claims

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for carers if we're smart about it. At work I'd offer to show anyone how I do my notes, because the agency will push it on us anyway. Online I'd say the office jobs are changing and that's just how markets work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency office would shrink and the rota would be done by software, which I'd actually welcome. My own work is hands-on, so it's years before a robot does a night sit. If anything, being the carer who's good with the tech makes me more useful, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager whether I could be the one who trains the others on the new apps, maybe for an extra pound an hour. I'd also start a little side thing, setting up video calls and reminder apps for clients' families, at twenty an hour on my days off. And I'd keep the savings ticking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a little guilt about the office girls. It feels like my sort of world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilt about the office staff. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lorraine, who does our rota, she's been there since before I started. She's not a computer person at all, and if the software does her job, I'm not sure what she'd do. I'd offer to show her things, but you can't make someone want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is Pete's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His route would be planned by software, which it partly is already, and he'd probably be pushed to do more drops an hour. That's annoying but it isn't the end of his job, because someone still has to carry the parcel up the stairs. It'd be him grumbling at dinner, not him out of work.

say: This is **good news** for carers who are smart about it.
Office jobs changing is **how markets work**, and I'd say so online.
think: Software doing the **rota** is something I'd welcome, not fear.
Being the carer who's **good with tech** makes me more useful, not less.
do: Ask the manager to **train colleagues** on the new apps for an **extra pound** an hour.
Set up **video calls and reminders** for clients' families at £20 an hour on days off.
Keep the **savings** ticking over each month.
feel: **Excited**, mostly, with some **guilt** about the office staff.
S1.quote: Being the carer who's good with the tech makes me more useful, not less.
fieldNote: She treats the change as a chance to **earn more**, both inside the agency and on the side.
Her free-market view shows in how she accepts **office cuts** as normal, though she feels guilty.
She expects Pete's van job to get **more intense**, not disappear, in this picture.

steps.text: Offer to train colleagues on the new apps for extra pay
Charge 20 an hour setting up video calls for clients' families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud, that people who adapt fast will be fine and the rest need help to get there. At chapel I'd say families should step up for their old people, not wait for the council. Online I'd probably post about which home robots look any good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a lot scarier than I'd admit. Robots in 2031 means both my care job and Pete's van job go in roughly the same year, and that's the whole household. I'd be thirty-two, with no degree and five months of savings, which isn't much against that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd register as a self-employed carer and take private clients at weekends, so I've got my own customers before the agencies switch to robots. Pete and I would save every penny of his overtime, and we'd put off trying for a baby until the money's clearer. Once the robots came, I'd want to be the person families pay to run and check the robot in their mum's house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a kind of buzz underneath. Frightened for us, but I can see a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028, three years before the robots. What does that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the AI does the notes, the rota and the families' questions, which is the desk part of my job, so I'd lose nothing much there. I'd use those three years to build my own little list of clients. When the robots come in 2031, families who already trust me might pay me to supervise one rather than trust a company they've never met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off a baby. How did that conversation go with Pete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be quiet about it, he's the one who wants kids sooner. I'd tell him I want a baby in a house where we know the rent is paid. Pete would say his mum had him with nothing, and I'd say his mum also never had a robot after her job.

say: People who **adapt fast** will be fine; the rest need help getting there.
Families should **step up** for their old people instead of waiting for the council.
think: Robots in **2031** take my care job and **Pete's van job** together.
Five months' savings and **no degree** isn't much against losing both wages.
do: Register as **self-employed** and take private clients at weekends now.
Save all of **Pete's overtime** and put off trying for a baby.
Aim to be the person families pay to **supervise the robot** at home.
feel: **Frightened** for the household, with a **buzz** of seeing an opening.
S2.quote: I want a baby in a house where we know the rent is paid.
fieldNote: Her calm public line hides a real fear: **both household wages** fall in the same year.
She uses the **three-year gap** to build her own client list before robots arrive.
The **baby decision** is where the fear shows, and it's a sore point with Pete.

steps.text: Register as self-employed and take private weekend clients
Save all of Pete's overtime towards a cushion
Put off trying for a baby until income is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and it's on each of us to use it. At work I'd tell the younger carers to learn the tech now and not wait to be pushed. I'd say the same to Pete's mates at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one feels doable. AGI in 2031 and robots around 2034 means I'd be thirty-five, with time to build something. What worries me is Pete, because he's slower to change than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the evening course in care management the college runs, so I could register a small agency of my own by about 2030. I'd put a bit of savings into a business account and start with three or four private clients. And I'd push Pete to get his van mechanic's certificate, because somebody will have to fix delivery robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but busy, if that makes sense. I like having a plan to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own agency, when the big companies will have the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the big companies treat families like numbers, and that's the gap. A small agency that says a real person checks every visit, robot or not, will sell in a retirement town. I'd rather own a small care agency than be let go from a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Pete doesn't want to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to carry more of the money for a while, which scares me a bit. I'd sit him down with the numbers on a Sunday, not nag. He listens to his dad, so I'd probably get his dad to say it.

say: **Five years** is fair warning, and it's on each of us to use it.
Younger carers should **learn the tech** now instead of waiting to be pushed.
think: This picture feels **doable**: I'd be thirty-five, with time to build something.
My worry is **Pete**, who is slower to change than I am.
do: Take the college's evening **care management course** to open an agency by 2030.
Put savings into a **business account** and start with three or four private clients.
Push Pete towards a **van mechanic's certificate** for repairing delivery robots.
feel: **Uneasy** but busy, and glad to have **a plan**.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a small care agency than be let go from a big one.
fieldNote: Five years' warning turns her into an **aspiring owner**, not just a worker.
Her pitch is **human checks** on every visit, aimed at families in a retirement town.
Her real risk is **Pete's reluctance**, which she'd tackle through his dad.

steps.text: Take the college's evening care management course
Open a business account and fund it from savings
Take on three or four private clients alongside agency work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone in care who doesn't plan with it is making a choice. At work I'd say it kindly. At chapel I'd say families have a decade to sort out who looks after their parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one I'd want. Robots in 2039 means I'd be forty, with a business that's ten years old by then if I start soon. I could be the one buying the robots, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the management course next year and open a small agency within three or four years, with two or three carers I trust. I'd test the first care robots as soon as they're sold, maybe for lifting and night checks, while my people do the talking. And Pete and I would try for a baby around thirty, because there'd be time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful. It feels like a ladder rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd test robots early. Wouldn't that put carers like you out of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes, I won't pretend otherwise. But if I use a robot for the lifting and the night checks, my carers can do the bit families actually pay for, which is the company and the care. Somebody's going to run those care robots, and I'd rather it was someone who's done a night sit herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first year look like, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course on Tuesday nights, savings into the business account every month, and two private clients at weekends to learn how to bill properly. I'd ask Lorraine to help with the books, actually, if the software's taken her job by then. That'd be nice, giving her work back.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and not planning with it is a choice.
Families have **a decade** to sort out who looks after their parents.
think: Robots in **2039** come when my business could be **ten years old**.
I could be the one **buying the robots**, not the one replaced by them.
do: Start the **management course** next year and open a small agency within four years.
Test the first **care robots** for lifting and night checks once they're sold.
Try for **a baby** around thirty, since there's time.
feel: **Calm** and **hopeful**, like climbing a ladder rather than facing a cliff.
S4.quote: Somebody's going to run those care robots, and I'd rather it was someone who's done a night sit herself.
fieldNote: A decade of warning makes her an **owner** who'd buy robots rather than fear them.
She's open that robots will **replace some carers**, and doesn't dress it up.
Her plan to **hire Lorraine** back shows loyalty alongside the market thinking.

steps.text: Open a small care agency with two or three trusted carers
Trial care robots for lifting and night checks once sold
Try for a baby with Pete around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Pete and I could both lose our jobs in the same year, and that's our whole income. What would help is cheap business loans and simple rules for small care firms, so people like me can start up instead of signing on. Less red tape, more chances.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the old people would choose, and I think a lot of them would take a robot for the lifting if it meant keeping their own carer for the chat. Nobody wants a stranger washing them, robot or person. Ask them that.

headlineQuote: Nobody wants a stranger washing them, robot or person.
portrait: Olga, 27, does **dementia care** and night sits for a seaside agency, and lives with her partner Pete.
She uses **AI every day**, for voice notes, side-effect checks and a client's memory book.
She's calm when little changes and sees **Steady Disruption** as a chance to earn more.
Fast AGI scares her because her job and **Pete's van job** would go together.
With more warning she plans to **own a small agency** that uses robots for lifting.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household wages could vanish in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** and simple rules so small care firms can start up.
